query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A pre-oxidation surface treatment with a dilute fluorine-containing solution will promote preferential oxidation of the available aluminum in a refractory high-entropy alloy, leading to a continuous and adherent Al2O3 scale that significantly reduces oxygen uptake during extreme high-temperature exposure by enriching the near-surface aluminum concentration.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., Nb-, Ta-, or Mo-based with a modest level of alloyed Al) having a standard, polished surface finish and no pre-existing protective oxide scale.
generation.intervention: Application of a surface fluorine treatment (such as dipping or spraying with an NH4F or HF solution) prior to high-temperature service.
generation.conditions: Exposure to dry air at service high temperatures for prolonged durations representative of extreme-temperature structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, continuous, and adherent Al2O3 film on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Fluorine reacts with surface Al to temporarily form aluminum fluorides that volatilize, thereby concentrating Al at the near-surface region. Upon subsequent exposure to oxygen at high temperature, this local Al enrichment drives the selective oxidation to form a protective Al2O3 layer, which acts as an effective barrier against further oxygen ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fluorine-treated samples will exhibit significantly reduced oxidation mass gain and improved integrity of the oxide scale compared to untreated samples under identical high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: An untreated refractory high-entropy alloy exposed to the same high-temperature, oxidizing conditions, resulting in a less-protective, mixed or non-uniform oxide scale with higher total oxygen uptake.
generation.boundary: The improvement may depend on the alloy’s aluminum content and the specifics of the fluorine treatment; if the Al content is below a threshold or the treatment parameters are not optimized, the effect may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of oxidation resistance improvement in refractory high-entropy alloys via fluorine treatment is uncertain due to compositional and microstructural differences relative to already studied systems such as TiAl alloys. Further investigation is needed to quantify the effect and assess any impacts on mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical refractory high-entropy alloy specimens. Treat one set with a dilute fluorine solution via dipping/spraying, while leaving the other set untreated. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation in flowing dry air at 1100 °C for 100 hours. Post-exposure, measure the oxidation mass gain and examine the surface and cross-section oxide scales using SEM and XRD.
measurements: Phase identification and continuity of the oxide scale via XRD
Morphological assessment of the oxide scale using SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fluorine-treated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in mass gain (or improved oxide continuity and adherence) compared to the untreated specimens, or if no continuous Al2O3 scale is observed, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In-depth analyses of the anti-oxidation behavior and structure of γ-TiAl alloys are of great significant for their maintenance and repair in engineering applications. In this work, fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects were prepared by isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C. Several characterization methods, including SEM, EDS, XRD and TEM, were used to evaluate the surface microstructure of the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects. The results indicate that the fluorine promoted the formation of an outer protective film of Al2O3, which significantly improved the oxidation resistance. The microcracks of oxidized specimens with the artificial defects provided a rapid diffusion passage for Ti and O elements during the 1000 °C/2 h isothermal oxidation treatment process, resulting in the quick growth of TiO2 toward the outside. The fine Al2O3 constituted a continuous film after the 1000 °C/100 h isothermal oxidation treatment. In this study, we executed a simple and effective strategy involving a two-step spraying and oxidation process to produce Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys with a dense Al2O3 film for application at high temperatures. The main results are as follows: (1)The oxidation resistance was significantly improved due to the formation of a protective Al2O3 film induced by the fluorine effect during isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C (6.03 mg/cm2 weight gain for the bare Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys, but 0.81 mg/cm2 for the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys).(2)The Ti diffused along the artificial microcracks, resulting in a quick growth of TiO2 in a short time (2 h), while a continuous Al2O3 film was generated underneath the oxide scale during further isothermal oxidation (100 h).(3)The Al2O3 particles between the alloy and continuous Al2O3 film were reflected in the γ-TiAl and α2-Ti3Al phases, which improved the adhesion of the oxide scale (fluorine-treated specimen had a deep yellow oxide scale on the surface without any exfoliation). These findings represent significant progress towards reducing the high temperature oxidation resistance of TiAl intermetallics by surface fluorine modification.
